name: Canada's National AI Literacy Initiative (AI for All)
short: AI for All: understand, use, build
status: Canada has no official five-area employer rubric. This version is our mapping: the national Understand, Use, Build progression, with the five skill areas used in the role matrix placed inside it.

groups.label: Understand
groups.description: Assess AI-generated information, recognize risks such as bias, misinformation and privacy loss, and know when not to use AI.

groups.label: Use
groups.description: Apply AI confidently and responsibly in your work.

groups.label: Build
groups.description: For those who choose: build with AI. Mainly technical builders.

understand.label: Understand how AI works, and when not to use it

risk_framework: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (widely used in Canada)

resources.label: AI for All: Essentials for Canadians
resources.note: Free national course, offered through community organizations from December 4, 2026, with open online access to follow

resources.label: Job Bank Training Finder
resources.note: Short AI courses for workers and job seekers

resources.label: Canadian privacy law
resources.note: Federal PIPEDA, plus provincial laws such as B.C.'s PIPA, apply to personal information entered into AI tools

foundation_intro: Your sessions follow Canada's national Understand, Use, Build progression. For a shared foundation, add the free national course alongside your first weeks.

foundation.label: AI for All: Essentials for Canadians
foundation.where: Free and self-paced, through Job Bank's Training Finder and community partners, from December 2026
foundation.how: Optional: in weeks 1 to 5, spend about 20 extra minutes a week on the course, or do it in one sitting.

items: **Privacy law applies now.** PIPEDA, or your provincial law (such as B.C.'s or Alberta's PIPA, or Quebec's Law 25), covers personal information used with AI tools.
**Ontario, 25 or more employees:** public job postings must say if AI is used to screen, assess or select applicants (since January 1, 2026).
**Coming:** federal Bill C-36, before Parliament, would require plain explanations when an algorithm shapes a consequential employment decision.
